timeline.title: Foundations: grades, English, and activities
steps: Treat every class test and board paper as part of your application record: Ivy admissions offices weigh grades and subject rigor heavily, so aim for top marks from day one.
Build reading and writing stamina in English (news, novels, essays) — strong English is the base for TOEFL/IELTS, the SAT verbal sections, and the application essays themselves.
Pick one or two extracurriculars you can commit to for years (debating, volunteering, coding, sports) and grow within them; Ivies value depth and leadership over a long, shallow list.
Read the College Board's overview of the digital SAT so you know what testing in FSc Year 2 will look like, and try the Bluebook practice app when you are ready.
Keep your passport and board documents organized — you will need attested copies for applications later.
On the A-Levels route this year is AS Level: the same advice applies, with SAT/ACT prep running alongside your AS exams.

timeline.title: Testing and shortlisting alongside board exams
steps: Register for and take the digital SAT during Year 2, scheduling it away from board exams; Pakistani students register online through College Board's international testing page.
If you prefer, take the ACT instead — sign up through act.org; the Ivies accept either the SAT or the ACT.
Take TOEFL iBT or IELTS Academic in the same year, booked well before application deadlines; the Ivies accept both for English proficiency.

Build a shortlist of around 8-10 schools (reach, match, and safety) and check each school's current testing policy on its official admissions site — policies changed at several Ivies in recent cycles.
Keep board exams the top priority: strong FSc Part 2 marks still matter, and schools review your final results.
Ask your school to keep official transcripts and predicted grades ready, and identify two teachers plus your counselor for future recommendation letters.

timeline.title: Essays, Common App, and financial aid forms
steps: Create your Common App account, add your schools, and check each school's supplement requirements on its admissions site.

Draft your main personal essay from the 2025-2026 Common App prompts, which stayed the same as the previous cycle; the first prompt, for example, asks about a background, identity, interest, or talent so meaningful your application would be incomplete without it.
Write each Ivy's supplement essays separately — every school has its own short questions and the wording changes by year, so use the current prompts from each school's official admissions pages.
Invite your counselor and two teachers through the Common App recommender system, and hand each one a resume or 'brag sheet' so the letters are specific.
Start the CSS Profile if you will need financial aid, and note each school's financial aid deadlines and any extra forms on its financial aid page.
Use free official advising: EducationUSA Pakistan offers guidance for US applications from Pakistan, in person and online.

timeline.title: Deadlines, interviews, and decisions
steps: Track the 2025-2026 cycle deadlines: most early deadlines fall on November 1, 2025 and regular deadlines between January 1 and January 5, 2026 — Harvard's, for example, are November 1 (Restrictive Early Action) and January 1 (Regular Decision); confirm each school's own dates.
Submit each application before its deadline and check fee waivers on the school's admissions site if the application fee is a burden.
Respond promptly if a school offers an interview (see the Interviews section for which schools offer them today).
Finish and submit financial aid paperwork — the CSS Profile and any school-requested documents — by each school's aid deadline.
After submitting, keep your grades up and update schools with any new awards or results.
Decisions: early results typically arrive in mid-December and regular decisions in late March; compare aid offers carefully before accepting.

tips: The Common App personal essay uses one shared prompt set; the 2025-2026 prompts remained the same as the 2024-2025 cycle. The first prompt asks about 'a background, identity, interest, or talent that is so meaningful they believe their application would be incomplete without it.'
Tell one specific story about yourself rather than summarizing your CV — the essay is your chance to show who you are beyond grades and test scores.
Write several drafts and read them aloud; cut clichés and anything that a stranger could not learn about you from the essay alone.
Stay inside the word limit shown in the application form and write in your natural voice — admissions readers want authenticity, not a thesaurus.

Every Ivy also asks its own supplement essays (often 'why us' or community questions). Use each school's current prompts from its official admissions site — wording changes between years, so never copy an old prompt list from a blog.
Get feedback from a teacher or counselor you trust, but keep the voice yours; do not outsource the writing.
Give the essay at least as much time as test prep — for many applicants it is where a borderline file gets decided.
Ask teachers who taught you recently and know your work well — subject mastery and specificity in the letter beat the title or prestige of the writer.
Request letters at least 4-6 weeks before the earliest deadline and give each teacher a resume or 'brag sheet' of your activities, achievements, and goals.

Use the Common App recommender system to invite your counselor and teachers; most Ivies expect a counselor letter plus two teacher recommendations — confirm the exact requirement on each school's admissions site.
Prefer teachers from core academic subjects (English, math, science) — schools want letters about your academic work, not only your character.
Waiving your FERPA right to view the letters is generally expected; waived letters read as more candid.
Brief your recommenders on why you are applying to these schools so their letters fit each one, and thank them afterwards.
Harvard: alumni interviews take place where volunteer interviewers are available, and not every region has capacity — an applicant cannot request one.
Yale: applicants do not request an interview; selected applicants may be invited to talk with an alumnus or current student after applying.
Princeton: alumni interviews are optional and arranged after the Admission Office receives your application.
Dartmouth: offers optional alumni interviews only — there are no on-campus interviews.

Several Ivies no longer interview at all: Columbia stopped interviews in 2023, Penn ended alumni conversations starting with the 2025-2026 cycle, Cornell does not offer personal interviews, and Brown asks instead for a short optional video introduction of no more than 90 seconds.

Where an interview is offered, treat it as a conversation: prepare a 60-second 'tell me about yourself', know why each school fits you, and bring your own questions. Not having an interview never counts against you.
